messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 41

He tells me he’s been a fashion designer for thirty years. “I have a good eye,” he says, almost apologetically. “I can walk into a room and know exactly what everyone is feeling by how they hold their shoulders.” He pauses, rubs his thumb along the seam of his trousers. “It’s a useful skill. I thought it was just talent.”

We’ve been meeting for a few weeks. He’s fifty-five, divorced, lives alone in a loft in SoHo. The loft is meticulous—everything white and grey, not a thread out of place. He wears a charcoal sweater today, perfectly cut. His hands are steady, but his eyes move constantly, scanning the corners of my office, the window, the door.

He was six when his father first beat him with a belt. “My mother would leave me with him on weekends,” he says. “I learned to read his mood before he even walked through the door. The way he set down his keys. The sound of his footsteps. I could tell if it was going to be a ‘bad night’ by the weight of his breathing.” He learned to stand very still, to make himself small, to predict. That hypervigilance never left him.

In his twenties, he found fashion. “Patterns made sense. You could control the outcome. If you followed the lines, the draping, the seams—you got something predictable. Something beautiful.” He became known for his clean, architectural silhouettes. Reviewers called his work “disciplined” and “restrained.” He laughs dryly when I repeat that phrase. “Restrained,” he says. “That’s a nice word for it.”

His marriage ended ten years ago. His wife said he was unreachable. “I’d disappear into the studio for days. If she touched me unexpectedly, I’d flinch. I couldn’t explain it. I just needed space. She thought I didn’t love her. I think I did, but there was always this… wall.”

He describes it as a glass box he lives inside. He can see people, hear them, but he feels separated by an invisible pane. He doesn’t trust the touch of others. He avoids family gatherings. He has dinner with colleagues twice a year—always at the same restaurant, same table, same order. “If things change, I feel like I’m falling.”

Night is hardest. He wakes two or three times a week in a sweat, heart pounding, from dreams where his father is standing over him with a belt, but in the dream his father is faceless, just a shape of anger. He gets up, goes to his drafting table, and sketches until dawn. He says the sketching calms him, because he is putting order back into the world.

Two months ago, a young assistant put a hand on his shoulder during a fitting. He jerked away. His voice went sharp. He saw the assistant’s face crumple, and he felt a wave of shame so deep he couldn’t speak for the rest of the day. “I’m the one who’s supposed to be in control,” he says, staring at his hands. “I can design anything. But I can’t stop my body from reacting.”

He came to therapy because he’s tired. Because the vigilance is exhausting. Because at fifty-five, he looks at his life and sees a series of successful collections, a closet full of awards, and a calendar empty of people who really know him. He says he wants to learn how to let someone in, but the idea makes him feel like he’s standing on a ledge.

Right now, he’s sitting in the chair across from me, perfectly composed, but his left foot is tapping a rhythm against the floor. He is waiting for me to say the wrong thing, to be unpredictable. He is waiting for the blow that never comes, even though he knows, intellectually, it will not. But his body does not know. His body still remembers the belt and the footsteps and the weight of his father’s breathing, and it is ready.
